newsitem.title: CHINA: China stock markets in bull run on firm outlook.
newsitem.headline: China stock markets in bull run on firm outlook.

text.p: China's stock markets are on a new bull run which could last right through 1997 due to a feeling that this time the rises are based less on speculation and more on fundamentals, analysts said on Sunday.
The last market surge towards the end of 1996 was viewed as highly speculative and led to a sharp warning to investors from Beijing regulators in mid-December and a sudden slump in prices.

Share prices are now back to where they were before the slump, but the mood of the market is different, analysts say. Share price rises are now seen as being linked to China's healthy economic outlook, and to the improved prospects of many listed firms.

"There are wide expectations that the performance of listed companies will improve fundamentally this year," said an analyst with Shenyin & Wanguo Securities, China's top brokerage. "That has helped the markets."

The stock indices on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges have all risen strongly in the past six weeks and analysts say they are likely to continue to hit year or even record highs for the rest of the year.

At close of business last Friday, Shanghai's foreign currency B share index was up 12.48 percent to 73.494 points against a close on February 21 of 65.341, while the domestic A share index was up 24.29 percent to 1,321.586 points, its highest closing level since May 1993.

Stocks on the Shenzhen bourse in southern China followed a similar course, with the B index closing at 161.27 on Friday, up 9.3 percent from 147.5 on February 21. The A index closed at 464.02, up from 353.05 on February 21.
The analysts said they believed both Shenzhen's A and B share indices could breach their record highs of 201.87 and 502.77 points at some point during this year.
The gradual improvement in China's economy over the past few months, with inflation falling and credit controls easing somewhat, is seen as the main factor pushing up prices.

"A full recovery in the performance of listed firms has lagged behind the improvement of the national economy," said another stock analyst. "The impact (of better economic conditions) will only be fully factored into listed firms' results this year."

Analysts predicted that if 1997 interim reports confirm the expectations of an upturn in business, the Shanghai B share index could approach or break its record high of 105.78 points in August or September.
One indication of the more solid basis for the recent rises is the focus on blue-chip stocks, analysts say.

"A feature for the recent bull run is the rise in the stocks in blue-chip companies," said a second stock analyst. "This indicates the markets expect them to take the lead in an overall recovery this year."
China's retail price inflation fell to a year-on-year 6.1 percent in 1996 against 14.8 percent in 1995, and fell further to 3.1 percent in January and 2.9 percent in February.
Bank interest rates were cut twice last year, and Beijing has promised to cut bank reserve ratios sometime soon as part of a cautious loosening of monetary policy, analysts said.
China's listed firms as a whole posted poor results in both 1994 and 1995 mainly due to poor management and the impact of tight credit policies, analysts said.
Most listed firms have yet to post their 1996 results.
Analysts have said they expect the 1996 results to be an improvement over 1995, but they are looking to the 1997 results for confirmation of a turnaround.
